card.title:
Click Next on the product list.
Why does page 1 load again?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: setPage doesn't change page now. It asks for the [[next render]].

caption:
Call setState and use the value on the next line in your machine coding round, and the interviewer will click Next twice to show you why.

Look at the card. page is a constant inside this render. setPage(page + 1) doesn't change it. It asks React to render again with the new value. So the line below still reads 1, and page 1 loads a second time while the pager says 2.

The fix: work out the next value once and use it for both calls.

Even better, fetch in an effect that lists page as a dependency, so the request always follows the state.

React calls this "state as a snapshot". It trips up people who know hooks well.

Source: react.dev, State as a Snapshot.
why: Rule 6 interview hook + rule 2 product scenario with visible symptom; hooks topic from rule 22.

card.text:
No developer offer yet. Pick one:

A) Join a product company now in QA or support, and try to move into dev
B) Keep applying for developer roles for 6 more months

[[Which one, and why?]]

caption:
Both paths get people into developer jobs. They cost different things.

A gets you inside: a real codebase, real users, a salary, and teammates who can refer you. The catch: an internal move isn't guaranteed, and many companies set a minimum time in your current role before you can apply internally.

B keeps your title and your time focused on development: projects, DSA and interviews. The catch: six months with no income and no work experience, and interviewers will ask about the gap.

If you made either move, how long did it take, and would you do it again?
why: Rules 13-15: two named paths a 0-2 yr dev faces now, not run before; n147/n64 shape.

card.title:
Tap the Phone label.
Why does the Email field get focus?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: A hard-coded id repeats every time the component does. [[useId]] makes one per instance.

caption:
The AI built a reusable form field. On a page with one field it's perfect. Add a second one and tapping the Phone label puts the cursor in Email.

Look at the card. Every Field renders id="field". An id must be unique in the page. When two elements share one, htmlFor connects the label to the first element with that id. Both labels point at the Email input, and a screen reader finds no label for Phone.

useId gives each Field its own id, and the id matches between server and client rendering.

No id at all also works: put the input inside the label.

Source: react.dev, useId; MDN, The Label element.
why: Rule 6 "The AI built..." hook; forms/a11y pool (rule 22) with a tap-visible symptom (rule 4).

card.title:
The search box won't let you type.
Why?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: value makes React the owner of the text. Without onChange, [[nothing can change it]].

caption:
Give an input a value without an onChange in your machine coding round, and the search box ignores every key the interviewer presses.

Look at the card. value={q} tells React that state owns this text. After every keystroke React puts the input back to q. Nothing ever changes q, so it stays empty.

React even warns in the console: a value prop without an onChange handler renders a read-only field.

Two ways out:
value plus onChange, when you need the text in state (filtering as you type).
defaultValue, when you only read it on submit.

Pick one per input. Don't mix them.

Source: react.dev, <input> (controlling an input with a state variable).
why: Rule 6 interview hook; controlled-input topic from the brief lane, symptom visible on first keypress (rule 4).

card.text:
Open your live app.
DevTools → Application → Local Storage.

Is your login token sitting there?

[[Every script on your page]] can read it.

caption:
Anything in localStorage can be read by any JavaScript running on your page. That includes a third-party script, a compromised npm package, or code injected through an XSS bug (a hole that lets an attacker run their script on your site).

One injected line can send your users' tokens to someone else's server.

An httpOnly cookie is the common alternative: the browser sends it with requests, but JavaScript can't read it at all. Pair it with the Secure and SameSite flags.

It doesn't fix XSS. It stops XSS from walking away with the token.

Source: OWASP HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet (Local Storage).
why: Rule 17: self-check only for leaks; n90 (bundle leak, 21.6k) shows "your app can't keep a secret" lands.

card.title:
Every row is wrapped in memo.
Why do all 500 still re-render?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: memo compares props by reference. A new arrow is a [[new prop]] on every render.

caption:
The AI wrapped every row in memo to make the list fast. Type one letter in the search box and all 500 rows render again anyway.

Look at the card. memo skips a render only when every prop is the same as last time. onSelect={() => select(r.id)} creates a new function on every render, and a new function is never equal to the old one. So memo compares, sees a change, and renders every row.

The fix: one stable function from useCallback, and let Row pass its own id.

To see it, turn on "Highlight updates when components render" in React DevTools.

If your project uses React Compiler, it does this memoization for you.

Source: react.dev, memo (minimizing props changes).
why: Rule 22 perf with a visible symptom; rule 6 AI hook; memo is in the brief lane and unposted.

card.title:
Click Log in. The page reloads
and the form goes blank. Why?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Submitting a form is a [[browser navigation]] unless you stop it.

caption:
Forget one line in your machine coding round login form, and the page reloads every time the interviewer clicks Log in.

Look at the card. Submitting a form is a browser action, not a React one. With no preventDefault, the browser does what it always did: it navigates to the form's action URL, which is the current page when there isn't one. The page reloads, React state is wiped, and your login response has nowhere to go.

e.preventDefault() as the first line of the handler stops that navigation.

In React 19 you can also pass a function to the form's action prop, and React handles the submit without a reload.

Source: MDN, Event.preventDefault(); react.dev, <form>.
why: Rule 3: line 1 states the consequence (page reloads); login form is a rule 3 product; sibling of n151 form defaults (1.6k).

card.text:
Your internship ends with a PPO (pre-placement offer): ₹6 LPA.
Placements start next month. Pick one:

A) Accept the PPO
B) Decline it and sit for placements

[[What would you do?]]

caption:
Both are reasonable, and your college's rules decide a lot of it. At many colleges, accepting a PPO takes you out of placements, so check your placement cell's policy first.

A is a sure offer from a team that has already seen your work. You skip months of tests and interviews and can spend final year learning what that team uses.

B can mean a higher package or a role you want more. It also means trading a sure offer for a chance.

Things to weigh: how much you learned in the internship, the people on the team, and how many companies actually visit your campus.

If you faced this, which way did you go?
why: Rule 13: concrete money + timing dilemma (n64 ₹6 vs ₹9 LPA got 3.5k); PPO not run before.

card.title:
Tap Like three times.
Why does it still say 0?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: Changing a ref [[doesn't re-render]]. Changing state does.

caption:
The AI used useRef for a like counter "to avoid extra re-renders". That's exactly the problem.

Look at the card. likes.current++ really does change the number. Log it and you'll see 3. But changing a ref doesn't tell React anything, so the button never renders again and still shows 0. The next time something else re-renders the component, it jumps to 3.

If the value shows on screen, it belongs in state. Setting state is what triggers the render.

Refs are for values the screen doesn't show: a timer id, a DOM node, the previous value of a prop.

Source: react.dev, Referencing Values with Refs.
why: Rule 6 AI hook; refs are in the brief lane; symptom visible on screen (rule 4).

card.title:
Type one letter of your address.
Why does the field lose focus?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: A component defined inside another is a [[new component]] on every render.

caption:
Define a component inside another component in your machine coding round, and the input loses focus after every letter the interviewer types.

Look at the card. Field is created again each time Checkout renders. To React, a new function is a new component type. Same spot, different type, so React removes the old input and mounts a brand new one. The text survives because it lives in Checkout's state, but the focus and cursor don't.

Move Field outside Checkout. Now it's the same type on every render, and React keeps the same input.

The React docs call this out directly: don't nest component definitions.

Source: react.dev, Preserving and Resetting State.
why: Rule 4 bug visible on screen; checkout scenario (rule 3); rule 6 interview hook.

card.title:
Show only in-stock phones.
Why does every phone still show?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: An async callback returns a promise. A promise is [[always truthy]].

caption:
If await inside forEach ever caught you out, this is its sibling: an async callback inside filter. The in-stock filter keeps every phone.

Look at the card. filter keeps an item when the callback returns something truthy. An async function always returns a promise, and a promise object is truthy, even one that will resolve to false. So filter keeps everything, before a single stock check has finished.

The fix runs the checks first. Promise.all with map gives you an array of true and false, in the same order as phones. Then filter by index.

The same trap works with some, every and find.

Source: MDN, Array.prototype.filter() and async function.
why: Experiment: rule 23 sibling of the n137 await-in-forEach breakout (19.2k), same async-callback trap in filter.

card.title:
The OTP arrives by SMS.
Why can't the phone autofill it?

panels.label: AI-generated
panels.code:
<input
  type="number"
  name="otp"
/>

panels.label: What I'd merge
panels.code:
<input
  type="text"
  inputMode="numeric"
  autoComplete="one-time-code"
  maxLength={6}
  name="otp"
/>

card.note: [[one-time-code]] tells the browser this field wants the code from your SMS.

caption:
The AI built the OTP screen with type="number". It looks right, and users still have to open Messages and copy the code by hand.

Look at the card. autocomplete="one-time-code" tells the browser this field wants a code from an SMS. Safari on iPhone uses it to show the code above the keyboard, one tap to fill. Without it, the browser has to guess.

type="number" is the wrong type anyway. It adds spinner arrows, accepts e and minus signs, and ignores maxLength. An OTP is a string of digits, not a number.

inputMode="numeric" still gives phones the digit keypad.

Source: MDN, HTML autocomplete attribute; MDN, input type="number".
why: Rule 22 forms pool (inputmode/autocomplete from the brief); rule 7 stake: users copy the OTP by hand; India-heavy OTP flows.

card.title:
Click Add to cart.
Why doesn't the cart update?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Same array, same reference. React sees [[no change]] and skips the render.

caption:
Push into a state array in your machine coding round and the cart stays empty while the interviewer keeps clicking Add.

Look at the card. push changes the array in place. Then setCart(cart) hands React the same array it already has. React compares old and new state with Object.is, sees the same reference, and skips the render. The data changed. The screen didn't.

It gets more confusing later: the next unrelated re-render suddenly shows every item at once.

The fix is a new array: setCart([...cart, item]). Removing is filter, updating one item is map. Both return new arrays.

Objects work the same way: { ...user, name }.

Source: react.dev, Updating Arrays in State.
why: Rules 11-12: classic interview question and one of the 2 strongest topics, on Saturday 07:00 (weekend mornings 3/4 broke out).

card.text:
Type an email with no account into your Forgot password form.

Does it say "No account found"?

You're telling anyone [[which emails have accounts]].

caption:
That message lets anyone check, one email at a time, who uses your app. Attackers run lists of leaked emails through forms like this, then target the matches with phishing or password guessing.

The fix is one sentence: "If an account exists for this email, we've sent a reset link." Show it for every email, send the mail only when the account exists, and keep the response time similar either way.

Check your login form too. "Wrong password" and "No such user" leak the same thing. Use one message: "Email or password is incorrect."

Source: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet and Authentication Cheat Sheet.
why: Rule 17 leak-only self-check; auth-form leak like n151 (the only self-check above 238, 1.6k).

card.title:
Switch to the Delivered tab.
Why does it still show Pending?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: The array lists every value the effect reads. [[status]] is missing.

caption:
The AI wrote the orders fetch with an empty dependency array. Click Delivered and the tab highlights, but the list still shows pending orders.

Look at the card. The dependency array lists the values from your component that the effect reads. This effect reads status, but the array is empty, so React runs it once on mount and never again. Changing status re-renders the tabs, not the fetch.

Add status to the array, and every tab change fetches again.

The exhaustive-deps rule in eslint-plugin-react-hooks flags this as you type. Don't silence it.

Switching fast? An ignore flag in the cleanup stops an old response overwriting a newer one.

Source: react.dev, Synchronizing with Effects.
why: Sibling of n152 useEffect fetch loop (11.5k) with the opposite mistake; rule 6 AI hook; tab symptom visible.

card.title:
The cart is empty.
Why is there a 0 on the page?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: React skips false, null and undefined. It [[renders 0]].

caption:
Write items.length && in your machine coding round and the interviewer will point at the lonely 0 on the empty cart.

Look at the card. && returns its left side when the left side is falsy. With no items, items.length is 0, so the whole expression is 0, not false.

React renders nothing for true, false, null and undefined. It does render numbers. So 0 shows up on the page.

Make the left side a real boolean: items.length > 0 &&. Or use a ternary when there's an else branch.

The React docs list this exact case as a pitfall: don't put numbers on the left side of &&.

Source: react.dev, Conditional Rendering.
why: Rules 11-12: classic interview trap and second-strongest topic, on Sunday 07:00; visible on screen (rule 4).

card.title:
Open Change password.
Why is the New field already filled?

panels.label: AI-generated
panels.code:
<input type="password"
  name="current" />
<input type="password"
  name="new" />

panels.label: What I'd merge
panels.code:
<input type="password"
  name="current"
  autoComplete="current-password" />
<input type="password"
  name="new"
  autoComplete="new-password" />

card.note: [[autoComplete]] tells the password manager which field is which.

caption:
The AI built a change-password form with two plain password inputs. The browser sees two password fields, has to guess which is which, and can drop the saved password into the New field too.

Look at the card. autoComplete tells the password manager what each field is for. current-password means "fill the saved one here". new-password means "don't fill this one, offer to generate a strong password instead".

Use them on every auth form: current-password on login, new-password on signup and reset, and username or email on the email field.

One attribute per input decides whether password managers help your users or get in their way.

Source: MDN, HTML autocomplete attribute.
why: Forms pool (autocomplete from the brief), rule 7 stake on a login/account form; rule 6 AI hook.

card.title:
Add a Filters button.
Why does the whole page go blank?

panels.label: Common answer
panels.code:
<button
  onClick={setOpen(true)}>
  Open filters
</button>
// Too many re-renders.

panels.label: What gets you selected
panels.code:
<button
  onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>
  Open filters
</button>

card.note: onClick needs a function. setOpen(true) [[runs during render]].

caption:
Write onClick={setOpen(true)} in your machine coding round and the page goes blank before the interviewer can click anything.

Look at the card. The parentheses call setOpen right now, while React is rendering the button, not when someone clicks it. Setting state during render asks for another render. That render calls setOpen again. React stops the loop with "Too many re-renders", and without an error boundary the whole app disappears.

onClick needs a function to call later: onClick={() => setOpen(true)}.

Same rule for every handler with an argument: onClick={() => remove(item.id)}, not onClick={remove(item.id)}.

Source: react.dev, Responding to Events (pass the function, don't call it).
why: Rule 3: hook ends on the consequence (blank page); beginner-classic React event bug, not posted before.

card.text:
6 months before placements. Pick one:

A) Contribute to a real open-source project
B) Build your own project end to end

[[Which one, and why?]]

caption:
Both show up well in interviews. They prove different things.

Open source proves you can read a big codebase you didn't write, take review comments, and get a change merged by strangers. That's most of the first year of a job. The catch: your first merged PRs are usually small, and finding a good first issue takes time.

Your own project proves you can design something, ship it, and explain every decision. The catch: nobody reviews it, so bad habits survive.

If you've done either, what did interviewers actually ask you about it?
why: Rules 13-15: new dilemma (not startup/service, deep/full-stack, hike/senior, DSA/projects); max 3 career posts this week.

card.title:
Double-tap Pay ₹499.
Why did two orders go through?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: Disable the button [[while the request runs]]. Then make the server safe too.

caption:
The AI built the Pay button with a clean async handler. On a slow network, one impatient double tap places two orders.

Look at the card. Each tap calls pay() again. Nothing stops the second call while the first request is still running, so placeOrder runs twice.

The fix on the client is a busy flag. Set it before the request, disable the button while it's true, and reset it in finally so a failed payment can be tried again.

That's only half. A disabled button won't stop a network retry or a second tab. The server also needs an idempotency key, so the same order is processed only once.

Source: MDN, HTML attribute: disabled.
why: Rule 7 money stake on a checkout (rule 3); state + form-submit lane; client-side sibling of the n95 idempotency post.

card.title:
Type the password, press Enter.
Why does nothing happen?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected
panels.code:
<form onSubmit={login}>
  <input name="email" />
  <input name="pass"
    type="password" />
  <button>Log in</button>
</form>
// login calls e.preventDefault()

card.note: Enter submits a [[form]]. A div is just a box.

caption:
Build a login screen out of divs in your machine coding round, and the interviewer's first Enter key does nothing.

Look at the card. Pressing Enter in a text field submits the form that field belongs to. The HTML spec calls this implicit submission. With no <form>, there's nothing to submit, so Enter does nothing. The Go key on a phone keyboard does the same thing as Enter, so it does nothing too.

Wrap the fields in a form, handle onSubmit, and call e.preventDefault() first. A button inside a form submits by default, so clicking still works.

One handler now covers the click, Enter and the phone's Go key.

Source: MDN, The Form element; HTML Standard, implicit submission.
why: Forms pool (form submit from the brief); login scenario (rule 3) with a keyboard-visible symptom, like n161 (13.2k).

card.text:
Copy a password and paste it into your own login form.

Did it work?

If you blocked paste, you also blocked [[password managers]].

caption:
Some apps block paste on password fields with onPaste={(e) => e.preventDefault()}, usually "for security".

It doesn't add security. It punishes people who use long, random passwords from a password manager, so they switch to something short they can type.

NIST's digital identity guidelines say services should let users paste into password fields, for exactly this reason.

The same goes for "Confirm email" fields that block paste. Users retype, make a typo, and never get your emails.

Remove the handler and let the password manager do its job.

Source: NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines (password verifiers).
why: Rule 17: user-facing failure on a login form; auth-form self-check like n151, the best self-check so far.

card.title:
The email is right there on screen.
Why is it missing from the request?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge
panels.code:
<input value={form.name}
  onChange={(e) => setForm((f) => ({
    ...f,
    name: e.target.value,
  }))} />

card.note: useState's setter [[replaces]] the object. It doesn't merge.

caption:
The AI built a signup form with one state object. Type your email, then your name, and the request goes out with no email.

Look at the card. The setter from useState replaces the whole object. It doesn't merge. setForm({ name }) leaves a form with only name in it, so email is gone from state.

The input still shows the email because form.email is now undefined, so React stops controlling that field. The console says so: "A component is changing a controlled input to be uncontrolled."

The fix: copy the old fields first, setForm((f) => ({ ...f, name: value })).

Class components merged this.setState for you. Hooks don't.

Source: react.dev, Updating Objects in State.
why: Rule 7 stake (backend gets a signup with no email); state + controlled-input lane; rule 6 AI hook.

card.title:
Tab through your login form.
Where did the focus go?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: :focus-visible shows the ring for [[keyboard users]], not for every mouse click.

caption:
Remove the focus outline in your machine coding round and the accessibility follow-up comes next: "now use it with only the keyboard."

Look at the card. *:focus { outline: none } hides the focus ring everywhere. Mouse users don't notice. Keyboard users press Tab and can't tell which field or button they're on.

:focus-visible lets the browser decide when the ring is useful. It shows when you Tab, and usually not when you click a button with a mouse. Text fields still show it on click, because you need to see where you're typing.

WCAG 2.4.7 (Focus Visible) requires a visible focus indicator for keyboard users.

Source: MDN, :focus-visible.
why: Accessibility follow-up after the n161 div-as-button breakout (13.2k); rule 7 stake = senior/a11y round.

card.text:
You have an offer from a big IT company. Joining date: "to be confirmed".

Pick one:
A) Wait for the joining letter
B) Join a smaller company now, for less money

[[What would you do?]]

caption:
Both are common choices, and neither is wrong.

Waiting keeps the bigger brand and the offer you already worked hard for. The catch: joining dates can slip by months, and those months show up as a gap on your resume.

Joining now means you start learning on real work immediately and earn while you wait. The catch: if the big company's letter arrives later, you have to choose again, and leaving a job after a few months has its own cost.

Whatever you pick, keep building and interviewing during the wait.

If your joining was delayed, what did you do?
why: Rules 13-14: first-offer timing dilemma many freshers face now; second career post of the Nov 30 week (rule 14: max 3/week).

card.title:
Pick a delivery slot.
Why can you select both?

panels.label: AI-generated
panels.code:
<label>
  <input type="radio" value="am" />
  Morning
</label>
<label>
  <input type="radio" value="pm" />
  Evening
</label>

panels.label: What I'd merge
panels.code:
<label>
  <input type="radio" name="slot"
    value="am" /> Morning
</label>
<label>
  <input type="radio" name="slot"
    value="pm" /> Evening
</label>

card.note: Radios become one group only when they share a [[name]].

caption:
The AI built a delivery-slot picker with two radio buttons. Click Morning, click Evening, and both stay selected. Nothing can unselect them.

Look at the card. Radio buttons become one group only when they share a name. Without one, each radio is its own group of one. Checking Evening doesn't uncheck Morning, and a checked radio can't be unchecked by clicking it again.

Add name="slot" to both. Now picking one clears the other, arrow keys move between them, and the form sends slot=am or slot=pm.

Keep each input inside its label, so tapping the word selects it. That matters on a phone.

Source: MDN, input type="radio".
why: Rule 3 booking/checkout scenario with an on-screen symptom (rule 4); forms pool; rule 6 AI hook.

card.title:
Open the filters popup, press Tab.
Why is focus on the page behind?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: A div modal is only a box on top. [[showModal()]] makes it a real modal.

caption:
Build a modal from a div in your machine coding round and the interviewer will press Tab. Focus walks straight out of it into the page behind.

Look at the card. A div modal is only a box drawn on top. Focus stays on the button that opened it, Tab moves through the page underneath, Esc does nothing, and a screen reader can still read everything behind it.

<dialog> with showModal() fixes all of that. The rest of the page becomes inert (not clickable or focusable), focus moves into the dialog, Esc closes it, and focus goes back to the button when it closes.

onClose keeps your open state in sync when Esc closes it.

Source: MDN, The Dialog element.
why: Forms/a11y focus topic from the brief; machine-coding classic (modal) with a keyboard-visible symptom, rule 6 interview hook.

card.text:
My 4 searches before I merge AI-written React:

1. useEffect → what's in [ ], and why?
2. set → a new object or array?
3. .map( → is the key from the data?
4. onClick → should this be a <button> or a <form>?

[[Search the diff. Don't just read it.]]

caption:
AI-written React usually compiles and passes the happy path. The bugs sit in a few predictable places, so I search the diff for them instead of reading it top to bottom.

useEffect: the array should list every value the effect reads, and the effect shouldn't run more often than the feature needs.
set: state must get a new object or array. A push or obj.x = 1 followed by a set call is a bug.
.map(: key={i} breaks the moment the list is reordered or an item is deleted.
onClick: a div with onClick should be a button, and a click that sends form data usually belongs in onSubmit.

What would your fifth search be?

Source: react.dev, Rules of Hooks and Updating Arrays in State.
why: Rule 16: AI take with a specific named workflow (4 diff searches), built from this lane's cards; n66 AI take got 14k.

card.title:
Turn on VoiceOver, tap the cart.
Why does it only say "button"?

panels.label: AI-generated
panels.code:
<button onClick={openCart}>
  <CartIcon />
</button>

panels.label: What I'd merge
panels.code:
<button onClick={openCart}
  aria-label="Open cart">
  <CartIcon aria-hidden="true" />
</button>

card.note: An icon has no text, so the button has [[no name]]. aria-label gives it one.

caption:
The AI built a clean header with icon-only buttons. Sighted users see a cart. A screen reader user hears "button" and has to guess what it does.

Look at the card. A button's accessible name (what screen readers read out) comes from its text. An SVG icon has no text, so the button has no name.

aria-label="Open cart" gives it one. aria-hidden="true" on the icon (passed through to the svg) stops the screen reader from trying to read the drawing itself.

If you can, show visible text next to the icon. It helps everyone, and the text becomes the name without any ARIA.

Quick check: turn on VoiceOver or TalkBack and swipe through your header.

Source: MDN, aria-label.
why: Accessibility sibling of n161 (13.2k); rule 6 AI hook; symptom audible in 30 seconds with a screen reader.

card.title:
Added one console.log.
Why did the product page break?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: A response body is a stream. You can [[read it once]].

caption:
Log a fetch response the quick way in your machine coding round and the page breaks the moment you add the log.

Look at the card. A response body is a stream. res.json() reads it to the end, and once it's read, it's gone. The second res.json() throws a TypeError (Chrome says "body stream already read"), so data is never set and nothing renders.

Fix: read the body once into a variable, then log the variable. If you really need two reads, call res.clone() before the first one.

The same rule applies to res.text() and res.blob(). Any two reads of one body fail.

Source: MDN, Response.bodyUsed and Response.clone().

card.title:
The CORS error is gone.
Why is the product list empty?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: no-cors doesn't skip CORS. It gives you an [[opaque]] response you can't read.

caption:
The AI fixed the CORS error in one line. The error is gone, and so is your data.

Look at the card. mode: 'no-cors' doesn't turn CORS off. It tells the browser: send the request, I won't read the answer. You get an opaque response: status 0, no readable body, no headers. res.json() then fails on the empty body.

CORS is enforced by the browser, and only the server can relax it. The server has to send Access-Control-Allow-Origin with your site's origin. In development, a dev-server proxy (Vite's server.proxy) works too.

That's why the same API works in Postman and fails in your React app.

Source: MDN, Request.mode and Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS).

card.title:
Type "react" fast.
Why do results for "re" show up?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Responses don't arrive in order. The cleanup [[ignores the stale one]].

caption:
Build a search box in your machine coding round without this and the interviewer will type fast, on purpose.

Look at the card. Every keystroke starts a request, and they don't come back in order. If the request for "re" is slower than the one for "react", it arrives last and overwrites the right results.

The fix is the cleanup function. When q changes, React runs the previous effect's cleanup, which sets ignore = true for the old request. Its late answer is thrown away.

AbortController goes one step further: call abort() in the cleanup and the old request is cancelled.

Source: react.dev, useEffect (Fetching data with Effects).

show yesterday's date. Why?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: toISOString is always [[UTC]]. Before 5:30 AM IST, UTC is still on yesterday.

caption:
The AI built an order history page. Orders placed between midnight and 5:30 AM show up under yesterday.

Look at the card. toISOString() always returns the time in UTC. IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead, so at 00:30 IST on 5 December, UTC is still 7:00 PM on 4 December. slice(0, 10) cuts out that UTC date.

Fix: format the date in the user's time zone. toLocaleDateString with the en-CA locale gives YYYY-MM-DD, and the timeZone option picks the zone.

Your tests pass all day and fail only at night, which is why this one ships.

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: sort changes the array [[in place]]. Same array, so React skips the render.

caption:
Sort a list this way in your machine coding round and the button does nothing. No error, no warning.

Look at the card. sort() doesn't return a new array. It reorders the same array in place and returns it. So setItems gets the exact array React already has. React compares old and new state with Object.is, sees the same array, and skips the re-render.

Fix: give React a new array. toSorted() returns a sorted copy and leaves the original alone. [...items].sort(...) does the same in older browsers.

reverse() and splice() set the same trap. Their copy versions are toReversed() and toSpliced().

Source: react.dev, Updating Arrays in State, and MDN, Array.prototype.toSorted().

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: The cache keeps the [[failed promise]] too. Delete it on error.

caption:
The AI added a cache to stop duplicate API calls. One failed request, and the profile stays broken until the user reloads.

Look at the card. Caching the promise is a good idea: two components asking for the same user share one request. But the cache keeps whatever promise it got, including a rejected one. Every later getUser(id) returns that same failure, even after the network is back.

Fix: when the request fails, delete it from the cache and rethrow. The next call starts a fresh request.

Book a slot for 5 December.
Why does it say 5 January?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Months in a Date start at [[0]]. December is 11.

caption:
Build a date picker in your machine coding round with this line and every booking lands a month late.

Look at the card. The string "2026-12-05" gives you 12 for December. But the Date constructor counts months from 0: January is 0, December is 11. So month 12 means "one past December", and JavaScript quietly rolls it over to January of the next year. No error.

Fix: subtract 1 when you build the date, and add 1 when you show getMonth() to a person.

The year and the day of the month start where you'd expect. Only the month index starts at 0.

Source: MDN, Date() constructor (monthIndex).

What I'd merge

The AI built a cart that remembers items across visits. It works for you. A first-time visitor gets a blank page.

What I'd merge

card.note: fetch has [[no timeout]] of its own. Add one, and stop the loader in finally.

caption:
The AI built the order tracking page. When the server gets slow, the loader spins forever and there's no way to retry.

Look at the card. fetch has no timeout option of its own. If the server accepts the connection and never answers, the promise stays pending, sometimes for minutes. setLoading(false) is on the line after the await, so it never runs.

get a white screen. Why?

What gets you selected

card.note: ?. only protects [[the one property]] right before it.

caption:

Look at the card. ?. only guards the property right before it. user?.address means "if user is missing, stop here". user exists, so JavaScript moves on, gets undefined for address, and then reading .city on undefined throws a TypeError.

Fix: put ?. before every part that can be missing, and give the screen a fallback with ??.

Don't sprinkle ?. everywhere to be safe, though. If a value must exist, a loud error finds the bug sooner than a silent undefined.

/orders/1042

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: parseInt stops at the [[first comma]] and returns what it read so far.

caption:
The AI built the cart total from the price text on the page. A ₹1,29,999 laptop adds ₹1.

Look at the card. parseInt reads digits from the start of the string and stops at the first character that isn't one. Here that's the comma after the 1, so it returns 1. No error, no NaN. Number('1,29,999') would at least give you NaN.

Fix: remove the commas before converting. Better: have the API send the price as a number (in paise) and format it only for display with Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN').

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Number-like object keys always come first, [[in number order]].

caption:

Look at the card. Object keys that look like whole numbers ("7", "42", "105") are always listed first, in ascending number order. Insertion order only holds for the other string keys. So Object.values gives you players sorted by id, not by score.

Fix: keep the sorted array for anything that has an order. If you also need lookup by id, use a Map. A Map keeps keys in insertion order, whatever they look like.

card.title:
Sort by price: low to high.
Why did the order not change?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: sort needs a [[negative number]] to move anything. true/false never gives one.

caption:
The AI built the price sort for a product list. The button works, nothing errors, and the list comes back in the same order.

Look at the card. sort() wants a number from the compare function: negative means a goes first, positive means b goes first, 0 means keep them as they are. a.price > b.price returns true or false, which count as 1 or 0. It never returns a negative number, so the engine is never told to move anything. In Chrome and Node the list stays as it was. Other engines may give a different, still wrong, order.

Fix: return a.price - b.price for low to high, b.price - a.price for high to low.

Source: MDN, Array.prototype.sort() (compareFn).

card.title:
The cart total says ₹NaN.
The check was right there. Why?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: [[NaN]] is the only value that is not equal to itself.

caption:
Check for NaN with === in your machine coding round and the error state you wrote never shows up.

Look at the card. A product with no price field gives 2 * undefined, which is NaN. Then total === NaN is false, always. NaN is the only value in JavaScript that isn't equal to itself, so that check can never pass.

Fix: Number.isNaN(total). Avoid the global isNaN() for this, because it converts first: isNaN('abc') is true even though 'abc' isn't NaN.

One widget failed.
Why is the whole dashboard blank?

What gets you selected

card.note: Promise.all fails if [[any one]] fails. allSettled reports each one.

caption:
Promise.all got the dashboard from 3 seconds down to 1. Then the offers API went down, and the whole page went blank.

Look at the card. Promise.all rejects as soon as any one promise rejects. You lose the user and the orders too, even though they loaded fine.

Promise.allSettled waits for all of them and gives you one result per promise: { status: 'fulfilled', value } or { status: 'rejected', reason }. Render what worked, and hide or show an error for what didn't.

Use Promise.all when the page is useless without every piece, like a checkout that needs both cart and address. Use allSettled when parts can fail on their own.

card.title:
The API was down for a minute.
Why couldn't it come back up?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: Retry a few times, [[wait longer]] each time, and add jitter.

caption:
The AI added retries so a failed request tries again. When the API went down, every open tab started hitting it nonstop.

Look at the card. The catch calls get(url) again straight away, with no limit and no wait. One failure turns into a tight loop of requests from every user. A server trying to restart gets buried by its own clients.

Fix: cap the attempts, wait longer each time (about 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s), and add random jitter so clients don't all retry at the same moment.

Retry only what can succeed later: network errors, 503, 429 (respect Retry-After). A 400 or 401 fails the same way every time.

Source: AWS Architecture Blog, Exponential Backoff And Jitter.

What gets you selected

Look at the card. setQ re-renders the component on every keystroke. Every render calls debounce() again and creates a brand new function with its own timer. The old timer is never cleared, so each keystroke's call still fires 300 ms later.

Fix: create the debounced function once. useMemo with an empty dependency array keeps the same function, and its timer, across renders. useRef works too, and React promises never to throw a ref away.

Writing debounce is a common machine coding question. Using it correctly inside React is the follow-up.

Fix it on the server. Send Cache-Control: no-store on pages and API responses with personal data, so the browser doesn't keep a copy. On the logout response, Clear-Site-Data: "cache" also clears what's already stored.

What I'd merge

card.note: setInterval [[doesn't wait]] for the last request. Late answers overwrite new ones.

caption:
The AI built live order tracking. On a slow network the status says Delivered, then jumps back to Out for delivery.

Look at the card. setInterval fires every 2 seconds whether or not the last request has finished. On a slow connection, requests overlap and come back out of order. An older request that answers late overwrites the newer status.

Fix: start the next request only after the previous one finishes. A setTimeout at the end of poll() does that: one request in flight at a time, always in order.

caption:

    .dataset.theme = localStorage
    .getItem('theme') || 'light';
</script>

card.note: The first frame is painted [[before your bundle runs]]. Set the theme before it.

caption:
The AI built a dark mode toggle. It remembers your choice, and it also flashes a white screen on every reload. At night that flash is the first thing users notice.

Look at the card. The browser paints the page before your JavaScript bundle runs, and useEffect runs after React has painted too. So the first frame always uses the light default, then the theme switches.

Read the saved theme in a tiny inline script inside <head>. It runs before the body is drawn, so the very first frame already has the right theme.

Next.js and other server-rendered apps hit the same flash. Libraries like next-themes inject this kind of script for you.

Source: react.dev, useEffect (runs after the browser paints).

card.title:
"Expand all" on 300 FAQs
lags for a second. Why?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Read, write, read, write: [[one layout per item]]. Read all, then write all.

caption:
Write this "Expand all" in your machine coding round and the follow-up is "open the Performance tab and explain the purple blocks".

Look at the card. Reading scrollHeight needs an up-to-date layout. Writing style.height makes that layout stale again. Do both inside one loop and the browser recalculates layout once per item: 300 FAQs, 300 layouts in a single click. That's layout thrashing (forced synchronous layout).

Read every height first, then write them all. The browser now does one layout at the end.

In the Performance panel it shows as a stack of Layout events with a "Forced reflow" warning.

Source: web.dev, Avoid large, complex layouts and layout thrashing.
why: Rule 22 perf-with-visible-symptom; interview follow-up stakes (rule 7) mirror n137 "follow-up question" hook.

card.text:
Save this as test.html and open it:
<iframe src="https://your-app.com"></iframe>

Does your app [[load inside the frame]]?

Then any site can do the same.

caption:
If your app loads inside someone else's iframe, that site can lay its own page over yours. It sets your frame to opacity 0 and puts a "Claim your prize" button where your "Delete account" or "Pay" button is. The user thinks they clicked the prize. That's clickjacking.

It hurts most when the user is still logged in inside the frame, for example when your session cookie is SameSite=None, which some embeds and single sign-on setups need.

Fix it with one response header:
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'

Use 'none' if your app never frames itself. X-Frame-Options: DENY is the older header that does the same.

Source: OWASP Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet and MDN, frame-ancestors.

The AI embedded the demo video.
Why is it a thin strip?

caption:
The AI embedded a product demo video on the landing page. It shows up full width and about 150px tall, a thin strip nobody can watch.

Look at the card. An iframe has a default size of 300 by 150 pixels. width: 100% changes the width, but nothing tells the height to follow, so it stays at 150.

aspect-ratio: 16 / 9 with height: auto lets the browser work out the height from the width, at any screen size.

Same fix for maps, Figma embeds and chart placeholders.

On slow 4G the headings stay
blank for 3 seconds. Why?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Without font-display, text waits [[invisible]] for the font.

caption:
Ship a custom font in your machine coding round, test it on slow 4G, and the headings stay blank while everything else has loaded.

Look at the card. Without font-display, most browsers hide text that uses a web font for up to about 3 seconds while the font downloads. That's FOIT (flash of invisible text).

font-display: swap shows the text in a fallback font right away, then swaps when the font arrives. If you'd rather avoid the swap jump, optional uses the web font only if it arrives almost immediately.

Google Fonts adds &display=swap to its CSS links for exactly this reason.

Source: MDN, @font-face font-display.

[[360px wide]]. Tab key only. Dark mode. Slow 4G.

The AI added a PDF button.
Why is the first load slower?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: Load a library [[when the click happens]], not when the page does.

caption:
The AI added a "Download invoice" button. Now every visitor downloads a PDF library on first load, including everyone who never presses it.

Look at the card. A static import at the top puts jsPDF in the same bundle as the page. It's a large library, and it has to download and parse before the page is ready.

await import('jspdf') inside the click handler lets the bundler split it into its own chunk. It downloads only when someone clicks. Vite and webpack both do this automatically for dynamic imports.

Check yours in a bundle analyzer: charts, rich text editors, PDF and Excel export are the usual suspects.

Source: MDN, import() and Vite docs (code splitting).

card.title:
The modal has a fade transition.
Why does it just pop in?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: display: none has [[no box to fade from]]. Hide it with visibility instead.

caption:
Toggle a modal with display: none in your machine coding round and the fade you wrote never plays. It just pops in.

Look at the card. While the modal is display: none, there is no box on the page, so the browser has no starting frame to animate from. It switches to block and opacity 1 in the same step, and the transition is skipped.

Fix: keep the box and hide it with opacity: 0 plus visibility: hidden. Opacity fades. visibility: hidden stops clicks, Tab focus and screen readers from reaching the invisible modal, which opacity alone doesn't.

Newer CSS can keep display: none and still fade, using @starting-style with transition-behavior: allow-discrete.

Source: MDN, @starting-style and visibility.

B) ₹12 LPA at a consultancy: a new client project every few months

card.title:
The AI built "redirect after login".
Why can it send users to a scam site?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: Only follow ?next= when it points to [[your own origin]].

caption:
The AI built "send users back where they were after login". Anyone can now use your real login page to send your users to their fake one.

Look at the card. next comes straight from the URL. A link like /login?next=https://evil.example logs the user in on your site, then redirects to the attacker's copy, which asks for the password "again". That's an open redirect.

A startsWith('/') check isn't enough: //evil.example starts with a slash and still leaves your site.

Parse it with new URL() against your own origin and only follow it when the origin matches. Everything else goes to the home page.

Source: OWASP, Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet.
why: Security in the 23:30 AI-built slot; leaked-password stakes (rule 7). Fix tested in node: //evil, /\\evil and javascript: all fall back to "/".

card.title:
Type in the search box.
Why does the chart keep flashing?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: lazy() inside a component makes a [[new component every render]].

caption:
Declare React.lazy inside a component in your machine coding round and the chart flashes a spinner on every keystroke.

Look at the card. Every render of Report calls lazy() again and gets a brand new component. React sees a different component type in the same spot, throws the old Chart away, suspends, and shows the fallback while it mounts the new one. Any state inside Chart is lost too.

Move lazy() to the top level of the module. It runs once, and Chart stays the same component across renders.

The import itself is cached, so the Network tab shows no second request. Only the flash.

Source: react.dev, lazy (declare lazy components at the top level).
why: Rule 22 React + visible re-render symptom; follows n152 (effect loop, 11.5k): a React pitfall the docs call out.

card.text: Set your profile name to: test Now check every place it shows up. Is it [[bold]] anywhere?

caption: If the name shows in bold anywhere, that screen is rendering user input as HTML. Swap for and the same spot runs an attacker's code for everyone who views it. That's stored XSS. React escapes text in JSX for you, so the usual culprits are elsewhere: the admin panel someone built with innerHTML, a toast library that accepts HTML, HTML emails, dangerouslySetInnerHTML for "rich" bios. Check the navbar, comments, notifications, the admin dashboard and the welcome email. Fix: render it as text. If you truly need HTML, sanitize it with a library like DOMPurify first. Source: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet.

What I'd merge

<header class="header">
  ...
</header>
<!-- sibling, not a child -->
<nav class="drawer">...</nav>

card.note: backdrop-filter makes the header the [[containing block]] for fixed children.

caption:
The AI gave the sticky header a frosted-glass blur. Now the mobile menu opens inside a 64px strip instead of covering the screen.

Look at the card. position: fixed usually means "relative to the viewport". But when an ancestor has backdrop-filter, filter or transform, that ancestor becomes the containing block. inset: 0 now means "fill the header", and the header is 64px tall.

Move the drawer out of the header so it's a sibling, and fixed is relative to the viewport again. In React, a portal to document.body does the same.

Modals inside animated cards break the same way.

Source: MDN, Containing block (identifying the containing block).

The AI added dark mode.
Why is the date picker still white?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: color-scheme tells the browser to draw [[its own UI]] dark too.

caption:
The AI added dark mode. The page is dark, but the scrollbar, checkboxes and date picker are still bright white.

Look at the card. Your CSS changed your colours. It didn't tell the browser anything. Form controls, scrollbars and the default page background are drawn by the browser, and it draws them light unless you say otherwise.

color-scheme: dark tells it to use its dark versions too. Put color-scheme: light dark on :root if you follow the system setting, or add <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> so it applies before your CSS loads.

Source: MDN, color-scheme.

card.title:
A long product name pushes
the price off the card. Why?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: Flex items won't shrink below their content [[unless you let them]].

caption:
Build a product row in your machine coding round, add one long product name, and the price disappears off the right edge.

Look at the card. Flex items have min-width: auto by default. For .info that means "never narrower than my content", and with white-space: nowrap the content is the whole name on one line. So .info refuses to shrink, the ellipsis never appears, and the price gets pushed out.

min-width: 0 lets .info shrink. Now overflow: hidden and text-overflow on .name finally have something to cut.

Same fix for chat previews, file names and table cells in flex rows.

Source: MDN, min-width (auto for flex items) and text-overflow.

card.text:
6 months before your first job. Pick one:

A) Build with AI coding tools: 5 projects, AI writes most of the code
B) Write it yourself: 2 projects, AI only to explain and review

[[Which one, and why?]]

card.title:
The AI wired up the chat widget.
Why can any site run code here?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: A message listener hears [[every window]], not just your widget.

caption:
The AI connected the help-chat widget to your page. Any website can now run JavaScript on it.

Look at the card. A message listener receives messages from any window that has a reference to yours, not just your widget. An attacker's site can open your page with window.open and post { type: 'OPEN', url: 'javascript:...' }. Your code assigns that to location.href, and the browser runs it on your origin, with your user's session.

Check e.origin against the exact origin you expect before you read e.data. Even then, treat the data as untrusted input.

Source: MDN, Window: postMessage() (security concerns).

card.title:
Looks fine on your MacBook.
Scrolls sideways on Windows. Why?

panels.label: Common answer
What gets you selected

card.note: 100vw [[includes the scrollbar]]. 100% is the space you actually have.

caption:
Use width: 100vw in your machine coding round, demo it on a Windows laptop, and the whole page scrolls sideways.

Look at the card. 100vw is the full viewport width, including the vertical scrollbar. On a MacBook the scrollbar usually floats over the page, so you never notice. On Windows it takes up real space, so 100vw is wider than the page by the scrollbar's width. That extra strip gives you a horizontal scrollbar.

For a block that fills its parent, width: 100% (or the default auto) already does the job.

Test on your Mac too: System Settings → Appearance → Show scroll bars: Always.

Source: MDN, CSS values and units (viewport-percentage lengths).

card.text:
Open a password reset link from your app.
Then open your analytics page report.

Is the [[reset token]] in the list of URLs?

caption:
Reset links usually carry a token in the query string: /reset?token=8f3a... Analytics tools record the full page URL, query string included, unless you tell them not to.

So everyone with dashboard access, and the analytics provider, can see working reset links until they expire. Same for invite links and magic login links.

Fixes:
Make tokens single-use and short-lived on the backend.
Don't load third-party scripts on reset and magic-link pages, or redact the parameter (GA4 has a setting for query parameters).
Swap the token for a session right away and remove it from the URL with history.replaceState.

Source: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet.

A long link pasted in chat.
Why does the bubble break out?

panels.label: AI-generated
What I'd merge

card.note: A URL has no spaces, so the browser [[can't break it]] unless you allow it.

caption:
The AI built a chat screen. Someone pastes a long courier tracking link, and their bubble pushes past the edge of the phone screen.

Look at the card. Browsers break lines at spaces and a few other break points. A URL has none, so it's treated as one long word and overflows max-width.

overflow-wrap: anywhere allows a break inside the word when nothing else fits. Use anywhere rather than break-word: anywhere also lets the bubble shrink inside a flex row, break-word doesn't.

Same bug in comments, usernames, file names and order IDs.

Source: MDN, overflow-wrap.

What gets you selected

card.note: At the end of a scroll box, the scroll [[passes to the page]] behind it.

caption:
Build a filter drawer in your machine coding round, scroll to the bottom of it, keep scrolling, and the product list behind it starts moving.

Look at the card. When a scroll box reaches its end, the browser hands the extra scrolling to the next scrollable thing, usually the page. That's scroll chaining. Users lose their place in the list while they're only picking filters.

1. await inside forEach
2. var in a setTimeout loop

card.title:
The AI preloaded the font.
Why does Network show it twice?

panels.label: AI-generated
panels.code:
<link rel="preload"
  href="/fonts/inter.woff2"
  as="font" type="font/woff2" />

panels.label: What I'd merge
panels.code:
<link rel="preload"
  href="/fonts/inter.woff2"
  as="font" type="font/woff2"
  crossorigin />

card.note: Fonts are fetched with CORS. The preload [[has to match]].

caption:
The AI added a font preload to speed up the first paint. The Network tab now shows inter.woff2 downloaded twice, and the console warns the preload wasn't used.

Look at the card. Fonts are always fetched in CORS mode, even from your own domain. A preload without crossorigin is fetched in a different mode, so the browser can't reuse it when the font is actually needed, and it downloads it again.

Add the crossorigin attribute with no value. Now the preload matches and the font downloads once, early.

Only preload the one or two fonts used above the fold. Preloading everything competes with your hero image.

Source: MDN, rel=preload (CORS-enabled fetches).

Why do they scroll away?

What I'd merge
